speaker: Mitchell Hashimoto
title: Mitchell Hashimoto’s new way of writing code
question: In early-stage tech M&A, why does an acquisition offer that is life-changing money for the founders often end up killing their product?
guest: Armon and I started getting cold feet because the way we described it is it's a dream-killing amount of money. Personally, it's so much money—your life could change—but you're too small to be important to a company like VMware. To them, it's meaningless. So this thing that we both were truly passionate about, the thing I wanted to work on more than anything else, would end in a sense because I would probably get thrown into working on ESX or something. The executives make it sound like they're going to do all this stuff with your products, but that's just one executive in a cog of corporate machinery. So we started getting cold feet, thinking: if they're interested, maybe we're onto something, and if we're onto something, do we want to sell out early in a way where our dream dies? That's why we called it a dream killer.

points.core: A modest purchase price makes the acquired product strategically insignificant to acquirers.
points.note: Accept: deal size is rounding-error small relative to the large buyer's revenue, so the product lacks organizational priority. Do not credit: generic statements about culture clash or bad management.

points.core: Sponsoring executives cannot override broader corporate machinery to protect small acquisitions.
points.note: Accept: pre-deal promises from one championing executive do not bind the wider acquiring organization after closing. Do not credit: claims that executives are simply lying out of malice.

points.core: Acquirers often reassign locked-up founders onto existing core products instead.
points.note: Accept: acquired founders are pulled onto the parent company's flagship or legacy teams during retention vesting. Do not credit: generic claims that founders lose motivation after getting rich.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the price that changes a founder's life is trivially small to the acquirer, and that asymmetry shapes everything that follows.

A $20–50 million offer can make founders personally wealthy, especially when they own most of the company and investors' preferences are small. For a large acquirer, though, that sum is a rounding error, usually justified as a way to hire a proven team rather than as a bet on the product. The deal is often an acqui-hire in substance, even when it isn't called one.

After closing, the incentives all point away from the product. The team gets reassigned to the acquirer's higher-priority projects. The product's revenue is too small to matter to the parent, so it loses internal fights for headcount and attention. It may also overlap with or threaten an existing product line, or need costly re-platforming onto the acquirer's stack. The executive sponsor who championed the deal often moves on. Founders, bound by earn-outs and vesting, tend to leave once those expire.

No one sets out to kill the product; it simply has no one left with both the power and the incentive to keep it alive.

The candidate describes the buyer redirecting the acquired team to its own priorities while earn-outs and vesting keep the founders tied to the buyer.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
The core reason is a stark asymmetry of scale. An exit of $15 million to $50 million creates life-changing wealth for early-stage founders who hold large equity stakes, making it rational to sell. For a multi-billion-dollar acquirer, however, that same purchase price is a rounding error—small enough to approve easily, yet too immaterial to command executive attention, sales distribution, or budget protection when priorities shift.

At these valuations, the buyer rarely values the standalone business. Instead, the deal is usually priced for engineering talent, intellectual property, or a feature to fold into an existing flagship platform. Keeping a small, separate product alive inside a large enterprise imposes heavy overhead—security reviews, legal compliance, brand management, and infrastructure maintenance—that dwarfs its modest revenue. Meanwhile, founders shift from existential urgency to time-based retention vesting inside slow corporate bureaucracy, losing autonomy while internal deal champions often move on. Because writing off a small acquisition costs the parent company almost nothing reputationally or financially, sunsetting the product and reassigning the team becomes the path of least resistance.

points.why: The response explicitly links the small deal size relative to the acquirer to the product's lack of organizational priority.
quotes: that same purchase price is a rounding error—small enough to approve easily, yet too immaterial to command executive attention, sales distribution, or budget protection when priorities shift.

points.why: The response says deal champions often move on but leaves unstated whether a sponsor's commitments can bind the wider organization after closing.
The response mentions founder retention vesting and team reassignment without specifying that the founders are reassigned to the acquirer's existing core products.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The money and the product's survival are separate questions. A sum that changes the founders' lives is usually a rounding error for a big acquirer, and the buyer rarely pays it for the product itself. Early-stage deals are mostly acqui-hires: the acquirer wants the engineers, the know-how, or the technology to fold into its own roadmap. Sometimes it simply wants to remove a potential competitor. A small product with a modest user base isn't worth the cost of keeping it running separately, bringing it up to the acquirer's security, privacy and infrastructure standards, or supporting it long-term.

Incentives make it worse. Founders' payouts usually come through retention packages and earn-outs that depend on joining the acquirer's teams and hitting its goals, not on keeping their old app alive. The deal also ends their control: after closing, the acquirer decides what happens to the product, so the founders can't really protect it. The usual result is a cheerful "our incredible journey" blog post, a sunset date, and users moved to the parent's product or left to find something else.

points.why: The response explains why a deal that is small to the buyer gives the acquired product little organizational priority.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: A price that is life-changing for early-stage founders, often in the low tens of millions, is usually a rounding error for a large acquirer, and that asymmetry of scale is what kills the product. At that valuation, buyers rarely purchase a startup to grow it as a standalone business; they are typically paying for the engineering team, a narrow piece of technology, or the removal of a future competitor. Even when an acquirer genuinely intends to keep the product alive, it collides with corporate materiality. Rebuilding a scrappy tool to meet enterprise legal, security, and infrastructure standards requires heavy investment for revenue that barely registers on the parent company's balance sheet, so leadership pulls the team onto higher-leverage core projects. Meanwhile, the founders lose control over roadmap and distribution, and their financial incentive shifts from fighting for product-market fit to vesting retention packages. Once the internal sponsor moves on or the founders finish their earn-outs and leave, the orphaned product becomes a maintenance liability and is quietly sunsetted.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The offer can be life-changing for the founders even if the product is a small bet for the buyer. The buyer may be paying for the team, the technology, or a head start on its own roadmap. It can get what it paid for by reassigning the engineers or folding the best features into an existing product.

Even if the buyer initially plans to keep the product alive, it still has to fund support, maintenance, and development. A small but loyal customer base can make that work worthwhile for an independent startup. Inside a larger company, the same product has to compete for staff and budget with much bigger businesses. Once the sale closes, the buyer gets to make that call. The purchase price is what it was willing to pay to own the company. The operating budget is what it’s willing to spend to keep the product alive.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
An acquisition offer can be life-changing for the founders even when the buyer has little interest in keeping the product alive. The founders are comparing a certain payout with years of risk. The buyer may value the team or the technology more than the standalone business.

After the deal, the product has to compete for engineers, sales support, and leadership attention inside a much larger company. Revenue that looked promising for a startup may barely register for its new owner. If moving the team onto the buyer’s flagship product promises a bigger return, the original product can lose the people who maintain it. The founders have already been paid and usually no longer control that decision. The buyer can get exactly what it wanted even as the product disappears.
